title: Andrey Markov's 1913 Analysis of Eugene Onegin
explainer: To demonstrate that his theory of chained, dependent probabilities applied to real data, mathematician Andrey Markov took 20,000 letters from the opening of Pushkin's 'Eugene Onegin' and counted how often a vowel followed a vowel versus a consonant — the first empirical application of what we now call a Markov chain. Every n-gram model and the 'Markov assumption,' that a sequence model's next output depends only on a limited window of prior context, traces back to this literary exercise in probability.

title: Chomsky's 1956 Hierarchy of Formal Grammars
explainer: In 'Three Models for the Description of Language' (1956), Noam Chomsky showed that no finite-state Markov process, however it is tuned, can fully capture the structure of English, and laid out a hierarchy of increasingly powerful grammar classes: regular, context-free, context-sensitive, and unrestricted. That hierarchy is still the standard way to reason about what a sequence model's architecture can and cannot represent, and it is the reason NLP needed more than simple n-gram chains to handle the structure of real sentences.
